The sixth wave was white.

They came down the stony slope at the top of the throat in the red moonlight, thirty of them, and at first Ye Feng thought they were the wolves of the first wave come back. Then they came closer and he saw the size of them. Each one as big as a pony, with a heavy silver mane over the shoulders and eyes like coals. They did not howl now. They came in silence, spread out in a long line, and the men on the wall who had laughed at the grey wolves at moonrise stopped laughing.

[Wave 6: the Silver-Manes.]

"Not like the first ones," said Saeli, very quietly.

Her arrow went out and struck the leader in the chest, and the great wolf stumbled, and got up, and came on with the arrow in it.

They did not throw themselves at the wall. They ran along it, testing, the way Ye Feng had once seen dock rats run along a quay looking for a hole. Then three of them went for the crack in the stone at the south end, where the bulls had broken it, all at once, and two of them were over before the spears could close.

One of them hit the man beside Ye Feng and took him off the step. The other turned on Ye Feng.

He did not try to kill it. There was no time to be clever. He put Moonripple's point in its face and kept it there, stepping back along the walk, and the great wolf snapped at the pale light and would not close, and Han Shuang's long spear came over his shoulder and went in under its jaw.

Down in the throat, the reserve had not moved. Ye Feng saw it, out of the corner of his eye, in the middle of everything. Four squads standing in their twelves with their shields grounded, watching the wall, waiting. Han Xin stood in front of them with his hands in his sleeves. The reserve does not move until the general moves it.

Qi Jiguang did not move it. The second watch closed on the crack with their shields, and Awang's broken stone was plugged with men, and Saeli's archers shot the last of the silver wolves off the slope one by one, three arrows each, four, five.

[Wave 6 cleared. Silver-Manes slain: 30.]

[Reward: silver-mane pelts, 30. Merit +25.]

[Wangyue: 11 wounded.]

The seventh wave came up the cliffs.

Nobody saw them come. The first anyone knew of it, a black shape dropped onto the firing step from the rock above the north tower stump, onto the backs of Saeli's archers, and an archer screamed.

Leopards. Spotted shadows, long and low and silent, coming down the cliff faces on both sides of the throat where no man could have climbed, and behind them, slower, heavier, the black bears of the deep hills, rearing up on the top of the wall with their claws out.

[Wave 7: the cliff hunters.]

It was the worst fight of the night so far, because it came from above. The squads were built to face forward. Now the enemy was on the step behind them, on the rock above them, in the throat among the men lying down to rest. A bear came down into the third watch where they slept and the whole watch woke at once and went for it with whatever they had in their hands.

Ye Feng found himself back to back with Bayu's old sergeant, in the dark at the foot of the wall, with a leopard circling them both. He watched its feet. It came at the sergeant. Ye Feng stepped across and put the blade between them, and the leopard twisted away from the light in midair, and the sergeant's spear took it in the side.

Maui pulled a bear off the wall with his bare hands and threw it into the throat, where twenty spears were waiting.

Yan Kui, among the prisoners behind the reserve, stood up and shouted something across the throat.

"The left cliff! There's a ledge! They're coming down the ledge!"

Saeli turned without asking who had spoken, and her archers shot along the ledge, and the leopards coming down it stopped coming.

[Wave 7 cleared. Leopards slain: 19. Black bears slain: 7.]

[Reward: healing salve, 100 jars. Merit +30.]

[Wangyue: 16 wounded.]

Maelis took the first jar of salve out of the panel's light before it had finished fading, and went to work.

The eighth wave was an army.

Not a broken one. It came down the valley behind a yellow banner on a tall pole, in step, three hundred men with shields of woven cane and long spears and good leather caps, and at their head rode a man in a yellow robe on a black horse, shouting the Heavenly Way in a voice like a temple bell.

[Wave 8: a Yellow Turban warband. Commander: a Heavenly General of the hills.]

"Real soldiers," said Qi Jiguang. "Good. They will stand still long enough to be hit."

He turned his head.

"Third watch up. Everyone up. Hou Cheng."

The deserter captain came forward through the reserve with his hands at his sides.

"You know these men," said Qi Jiguang.

"I know that banner. I ran from it in the spring."

Hou Cheng looked out over the wall.

"They will come at the gate in a block. They will not stop until the man in yellow stops. They think he cannot be killed."

"Saeli," said Ye Feng.

The warband came at the gate in a block. They were brave and they were drilled and they hit the wall like a fist, and for a long minute it held them only because Qi Jiguang's men had been drilled harder. Spears against spears through the gaps in the stone. Cane shields splintering. The yellow banner swaying over the press.

Saeli stood on the firing step, drew her bow to her ear and waited, for ten heartbeats and then twenty. The man in yellow rode up and down behind his block on the black horse, shouting. Once, he turned to face the wall and raised his sword.

She loosed.

The man in yellow went backwards off his horse with an Eldari arrow through his throat, in the middle of a word. The temple-bell voice stopped. The yellow banner swayed, and leaned, and went down.

The block stopped pushing. Men looked round for the voice. Then the second watch pushed back, all together, shields, step, and the warband broke from the front.

Eighty of them threw down their spears at the foot of the wall and knelt, and looked up at Hou Cheng standing on the walk above them, and Hou Cheng shouted down at them in the hill dialect, and they put their hands on their heads.

[Wave 8 cleared. Warband slain: 74. Laid down arms: 80.]

[Territory Defence: attackers who live have been won.]

[Reward: leather armour, 100 sets. Merit +30.]

[Wangyue: 19 wounded.]

The ninth wave was everything.

It came an hour before dawn, when the men on the wall had been fighting all night and the moon was low and red over the hills. The panel said only one word.

[Wave 9: the red-moon host.]

What was left of every wave came back at once. Grey wolves and the last of the raiders and the stragglers of the warband and things from the hills that had not come before, hunched shapes that might once have been men. They came at the whole length of the wall at the same time, from the north tower stump to the crack at the south end, and there was no rotating watches any more, because there was no one to rotate. Everyone was on the wall. Even the reserve.

Qi Jiguang moved it at last. He looked down at Han Xin in the throat, and Han Xin nodded once, and the four squads went up the steps at the run.

The gate broke.

Not the stone. The iron-banded timber in the middle, which had taken the bulls and the warband's block and the Silver-Manes, cracked down the centre under a battering of clubs and claws and fell inward in two pieces.

Hou Cheng was standing in the gateway before anyone told him to. Him and his hundred and forty, with the cane shields of the warband they had picked up off the ground, and no spears, because nobody had given them spears yet. They locked the cane shields across the gap in a curved wall of their own, and pushed, and held.

"Spears!"

Qi Jiguang's voice cracked like a whip.

"Give them spears!"

Somebody did. The rack behind the gate was emptied in a heartbeat, spears passed hand to hand over the heads of the men in the gateway, and Hou Cheng's broken soldiers, who had been the enemy at moonrise, held the gate of Wangyue with Wangyue's spears.

Two of Wangyue's own died on the wall that hour. A farmer from Little Elm, pulled off the step by something with claws. And a boy from the Commons who had come up with the water and would not go back down.

Then the sky over the headland began to grey, and the host began to thin, and Ye Feng, standing in the gateway behind Hou Cheng's shields with Moonripple running with pale light, heard Han Xin say, very quietly, behind him:

"One more, my lord."

[Wave 9 cleared.]

[Reward: seed millet, 100 sacks. Salt, 50 jars. Merit +35.]

[Wangyue: 2 dead. 23 wounded.]

The tenth wave was one creature.

It came down the stony slope in the red moonlight so slowly that at first Ye Feng thought it was a boulder moving. Then it stepped into the torchlight below the wall and he saw it.

It was a tiger, but not like any tiger he had seen in pictures. It was the size of an ox, its coat almost white in the moon, with black stripes like ink brushed on paper and a broad white blaze across its brows. Its eyes were gold, and old wounds crossed its shoulders, long healed. It did not roar. It looked at the wall, at the spears and at the archers, and then at Ye Feng, and he understood that it knew exactly who was in charge.

[Wave 10. MASTER OF THE HILLS: White-Brow, King of the Kunyu Tigers.]

"Bows," said Saeli.

The arrows went into its shoulders and stuck there and it did not slow down. It came at the wall in three long bounds and went over it, over the spears, over the firing step, as if the stone were not there, and landed in the throat behind the wall, among the exhausted squads resting at the foot of the steps, and they went everywhere.

Ye Feng jumped down off the wall.

He did not think. He saw the white shape among his soldiers and a man under its paw and he jumped. He landed badly, rolled, came up with Moonripple in his hand and the tiger in front of him, ten paces off, turning its huge head to look at him.

It came.

He had never been charged by anything that big. It was like standing in front of a falling wall. Back, he thought, and went back, and the paw went past his face with a sound like a sail tearing. Side. The second paw raked the ground where he had been. In. He cut across the inside of its foreleg, and the blade went in, and the pale light in it flared like a lamp.

The tiger screamed. It turned on him faster than anything that size should be able to turn, and its shoulder hit him and knocked him flat, and its jaws came down.

A spear went into its neck. Han Shuang's spear. She had come down off the wall after him, and she was standing over him with both hands on the shaft, screaming at the tiger in a voice he had never heard her use. The tiger reared back off him, and Maui came out of the dark from the other side and caught it round the neck with both arms, and held it.

Held it. For one long breath, the giant and the tiger stood locked together in the red moonlight, and the tiger could not move its head.

Ye Feng got up onto one knee and put Moonripple up under its jaw, where the white fur was thinnest, with everything he had.

[Souls: 13.]

[MASTER OF THE HILLS SLAIN.]

[Lord Ye Feng: Level 7 → 8.]

Maui let the tiger down very gently onto the stones, as if it were something he respected. Han Shuang pulled her spear out and stood with it in both hands, breathing hard.

"My lord," she said, "you jumped off the wall."

"It was killing someone."

"It was killing Lao Qi," said Han Shuang. "From Stone Gate. One of the boys who sat down."

She looked past him, to where the miller's son was sitting up against the throat wall, holding his torn arm and staring at the dead tiger.

"He'll live."

She stood looking at Ye Feng a moment longer, and her face did something complicated.

"My lord," she said, "please don't do that again."

"I can't promise that."

She wiped her face on her sleeve, which made it worse.

"I just needed to say it."

He went to Huang the next morning with salt.

It was a day's ride west along the coast road, the first time Ye Feng had gone further than Iron Ox's estate, and he took twenty of Zhao Mu's best riders, Kirana, Han Shuang, and three carts. Two carts of smoked fish. One cart of salt from Mak Senah's pans and the reward set. The white tiger's pelt rode in the storage pouch at his belt, with the four moon pearls from the bay and a jar of salt for the road. He did not mean to sell the pelt, but he wanted Huang to see it.

"Every lord on the server read the defence notice," Kirana said, riding beside him. "Every merchant in Huang will have heard of the lord who came first. Let them see the pelt. Let them understand that the lord who came first did not do it by hiding in his hall."

"And the salt?"

"Officially, it belongs to the throne," said Kirana.

She smiled a little.

"Unofficially, Huang has not seen a salt boat in a month, because the Yellow Turbans are on every road. Unofficially, my lord will be the most popular man in the market."

Huang was a real town, the first Ye Feng had seen in this world.

A wall of rammed earth and grey brick, three times the height of Iron Ox's, with a gate tower and soldiers on it in the red coats of the Han. A river beside it running down to the sea, with a stone quay and a dozen fishing boats and one bigger coaster with a brown sail. Inside the gate, streets of tiled roofs, the smell of cooking oil and woodsmoke and too many people.

Outside the gate, a camp.

Hundreds of people, perhaps a thousand, in shelters of mats and branches along the river bank below the wall. Refugees from the burned villages of the coast, waiting for the gate to open and let them in. It did not open. The soldiers on the tower looked down at them with the bored faces of men who had stopped seeing what they looked at.

Ye Feng rode past the camp very slowly.

"My lord," said Kirana quietly. "Not today."

"I know."

He kept looking.

"But they'll hear about the lord by the sea who has food."

"They will," said Kirana. "That is why I said not today. Today we sell."

They sold.

Kirana had been right about the salt. The carts were barely through the gate before a crowd had formed, and by noon there was not a jar left, and she had a purse that clinked and a second purse that clinked louder.

The smoked fish went nearly as fast. Kahu's gold fish, smoked in the new smokehouse, fat and firm, at a time when Huang had been eating river carp for a month.

The pelt they did not sell. In the square in front of the magistrate's yamen, Ye Feng opened the little grey pouch at his belt and drew the whole great hide out of it, yard after yard of white fur, while the people nearest stepped back and a child shrieked with delight. They spread it over an empty cart and let people come and look, and people came. White fur, ink stripes, the great broad brow. Children touched the teeth. An old man wept and said it had taken his son on the Kunyu road nine years ago, and he had seen it, he knew those scars.

Ye Feng stood by the cart and watched the crowd and kept his hand on Moonripple's hilt and said very little.

The pearl stall was at the end of the quay, where the market ran out, by the brown-sailed coaster.

It was hardly a stall. A board on two stones, a cloth, a few dull river pearls in a wooden dish, and behind them a very old woman on a stool with a heavy magnifying glass hanging round her neck on a cord.

Kirana stopped.

"My lord. That one."

The old woman watched them come. She had eyes like wet black stones, very bright in a face like a dried apple.

Ye Feng took a pearl out of the storage pouch, one of the four from the bay, and put it on her cloth. Even in the bright noon light it glowed, a soft silver light from inside, like a tiny moon.

The old woman looked at it for a long time without touching it. Then she picked it up, held it in the shade of her hand, and put the glass to her eye.

[Mother Lin. Han. Talent: Pearl Appraiser (A).]

[★★★★ · Path: none. She has looked at pearls for seventy years. Nobody alive sees them better.]

"Where," she said, very quietly, "did you get this?"

"The sea."

"Everybody's pearls come from the sea."

She turned it in her fingers.

"Not everybody's shine in the shade."

She looked up at him over the glass.

"I have seen two of these in my life. One in the magistrate's mother's hairpin, which her grandmother brought from the south. One in a dream."

She put it down on the cloth very gently.

"Fifty silver."

"That's all?"

"In Huang, that is all. In Linzi, two hundred. In Luoyang, more than you can count."

She looked at the brown-sailed coaster behind him, and at the men lounging on its deck, and lowered her voice.

"But you are not in Luoyang, young lord. You are in Huang, and if you take this pearl to the magistrate he will ask you where it came from, and then he will come and look. Sell it to me. I will tell no one."

He sold it to her. And a second one.

[Sold: moon pearl, 2. Treasury: 940 → 1,040 silver.]

"Come back when you have more," said Mother Lin, putting them away inside her robe. "But come back quietly. And next time, do not walk past that boat."

He looked at the coaster. One of the men on the deck was watching him. A small, weathered man with a crab-claw scar on one cheek, who looked away when Ye Feng met his eyes.

At the gate, as they were leaving, a young man stopped them.

He was very tall, taller than Han Shuang, perhaps eighteen, with a long serious face and a red sash over a soldier's coat that had been mended many times. He carried a long bow, unstrung, longer than any Ye Feng had seen, and a quiver of arrows fletched with black feathers.

"You are the ones who sold the salt," he said.

"We were," said Kirana. "It's all gone."

The young man's face did not change, but something in it went still.

"All of it?"

Ye Feng looked at him. At the mended coat, at the bow, at the way he stood, balanced, the way Han Xin stood. He felt the Eyes stir and he let them stay closed. He did not know why. Something told him this young man would feel it if he looked.

"Why do you need it?" he asked.

"For my mother." The young man said it simply. "She is not well, and the physician says she needs salt in her broth, and there has been none in the market for a month."

He paused.

"I am sorry. I should not have stopped you."

Ye Feng reached into the storage pouch. There was one small jar left, the one Mak Senah had packed for the journey, for their own food.

He held it out.

The young man looked at it, and then at Ye Feng, and did not take it.

"What do you want for it?"

"Nothing. It's for your mother."

The young man stood very still for a long moment. Then he took the jar in both hands, carefully, the way a man takes something he will have to repay, and bowed. Not a quick bow. A full bow, from the waist, the bow of a soldier to someone he has decided to remember.

"I will not forget this," he said. "My lord of the sea."

He turned and went back through the gate into the town, his long bow on his shoulder, and did not look back.

"That one sees," said Kirana quietly, watching him go.

"I know," said Ye Feng.

Chapter 67: The Lady of Langya:
The Langya ships came through the reef gap a little before noon, three of them, with green sails and a white plum blossom painted on each.

Ye Feng stood at the top of the harbour steps and watched them come in. He had washed his hair. He was wearing the boots. He had not told anyone why, and everyone in Wangyue knew anyway, and nobody had said a word about it to his face, which he suspected was Wang Meng's doing.

Behind him on the steps stood Han Xin and General Qi, and Wang Meng with his slates, and Kirana. A little further back stood Ye Tian, Ye Xing, Ye Shuang and Ye Chuan, side by side in their best armour, with faces so perfectly serious that he did not dare look at them.

"Brother," murmured Ye Xing, very quietly, "your collar."

He fixed his collar.

"Brother," murmured Ye Chuan from the other end of the row, just as quietly, "your boots are on the right feet. I checked."

Ye Tian, without moving his head, stood on Ye Chuan's foot.

Ye Wan'er, half hidden behind Ye Shuang, was not looking at the lady's ships at all, only at their waterlines.

"Low in the water," she murmured. "Salt fish and lacquer. They will want our cheese, Brother, and they will pay in pearls if you let me do the talking."

"Not today," said Ye Feng.

She agreed that it was not, and wrote something on her slate anyway.

The first ship came alongside the inner arm, and the Nacari on the harbour wall caught its ropes, and a gangplank came down. Three people came down it.

The first was a tall woman in plain grey armour with a long white staff in her hand, a staff with a spear blade at its head and a hook below the blade. She walked as if the stones of the harbour belonged to her, and her eyes went over every soldier on the wall and every boat in the harbour before her feet touched the ground. The second was a slender man in a scholar's robe, middle-aged, with a calm clever face and an ink brush tucked behind one ear, who looked at Mi Zhu's trading house first and the wall second.

The third was Aisyah.

She was not wearing armour. She was wearing a long green coat over a plain dark dress, with her hair covered by a light green scarf, the way the girls at his school had worn their scarves on Fridays. She was looking up at the wall and the towers and the long arms of the harbour with her lips a little parted, the way a person looks at something larger than they expected.

He knew her at once.

He had known, really, since the first Ranking, when he read her name and his hand closed on the wall so hard the stone bit his palm. He had told himself every time since that it was a common name. There had been three Aisyahs in his school year.

There had only been one who laughed like that in the corridor outside the library.

She came up the steps. She stopped two steps below him, so that their eyes were level, and put her right hand over her heart, and bowed her head a little, the way a lord bows to a lord.

"Lord Ye Feng," she said. "Thank you for the salt."

Her voice was exactly the same.

"Lady Aisyah," said Ye Feng. He heard his own voice come out steady, and was proud of it. "Thank you for the boots."

She looked down at his feet, and then up at his face, and for a moment there was something in her eyes, a small puzzled look, as if she were trying to remember where she had put something.

Then it was gone, and she smiled.

"They fit," she said.

"Like they were made for me."

She did not know him. He saw it, and understood it, and found that it did not hurt as much as he had always thought it would. He had been the quiet boy at the back of the class, the one from the children's home, who went to the library at lunch. She had never really looked at him then. She was looking at him now, as the Lord of Wangyue, and that was something, and it was more than he had ever had.
